title: An Algorithm for the Machine Calculation of Complex Fourier Series
access: Full. The complete five-page article by James W. Cooley and John W. Tukey was read from the official American Mathematical Society Mathematics of Computation PDF (vol. 19, no. 90, 1965, journal pp. 297–301; DOI 10.1090/S0025-5718-1965-0178586-1). The cached PDF and layout-preserving extraction are content/courses/digital-signal-processing/research/texts/cooley-tukey.pdf and cooley-tukey.txt, each with its own provenance sidecar. The paper has no titled prose sections, so pointers below use journal/PDF pages and equation numbers rather than invented section names.
topics: Historical and computational motivation (journal p. 297; PDF p. 1): Yates's 2^m factorial interaction method, Box et al.'s 3^m generalization, Good's sparse-matrix factorization, and the shift from N^2 to N log N work.

Complex Fourier-series definition and baseline cost (equations 1–2; journal p. 297; PDF p. 1): X(j)=sum_k A(k)W^(jk), W=e^(2pi i/N), with one ‘operation’ defined as a complex multiply followed by a complex add.

Two-factor decomposition (equations 3–8; journal pp. 297–298; PDF pp. 1–2): write N=r1 r2, split both indices into mixed-radix digits, compute an intermediate array A1, then finish with a second family of short sums.
Recursive mixed-radix factorization (equations 9–13; journal p. 298; PDF p. 2): N=r1 r2 ... rm, operation count T=N(r1+r2+...+rm), equal-radix form T(r)=rN log_r N, and radix-efficiency comparison.

Radix selection (journal pp. 298–299; PDF pp. 2–3): maximize the number of factors, compare r/log2 r for radices 2–10, and prefer powers of 2 or 4 on binary machines despite radix 3's small formal advantage.

Binary radix-2 index representation (equations 14–19; journal p. 299; PDF p. 3): express input and output indices as bit strings and successively replace one input-index bit by one output-index bit in intermediate arrays A_l.

In-place two-location update and parallelism (equations 20–21; journal p. 300; PDF p. 4): each stage combines pairs differing in one bit position, can update the same N storage locations, and permits independent pairs to be evaluated simultaneously.

Output order and radix-4 grouping (equation 22 and surrounding text; journal p. 300; PDF p. 4): the final transform appears in bit-reversed index order, while grouping two radix-2 stages gives an equivalent radix-4 algorithm.

Difference-equation application (equations 23–25; journal p. 300; PDF p. 4): transform a cyclic three-term difference equation, divide by its frequency response, and reuse bit-inverted arrays so a second transform restores natural order without a separate permutation.

IBM 7094 implementation and timing table (journal pp. 300–301; PDF pp. 4–5): measured times for one- and three-dimensional arrays of 2^11 through 2^13 complex points, followed by affiliations and two references.
key_results: Equations (1)–(2), journal p. 297: direct evaluation of all N complex Fourier sums requires N^2 complex multiply-add operations under the paper's operation definition.

Abstract and journal p. 297: when N is highly composite, the transform can be evaluated in fewer than 2N log2 N such operations while using only the N storage locations already occupied by the input coefficients.

Equations (3)–(7), journal pp. 297–298: for N=r1r2, mixed-radix index substitutions separate the original sum into r1-point inner transforms that form A1(j0,k0), followed by r2-point outer transforms that form X(j1,j0).
Equation (8), journal p. 298: the two-stage factorization costs T=N(r1+r2), because the N intermediate outputs each require r1 operations and the N final outputs each require r2 operations.

Equations (9)–(10), journal p. 298: recursively factoring N=r1r2...rm gives an m-stage algorithm with T=N(r1+r2+...+rm), exposing transform speed as a property of the factorization of N rather than only its magnitude.

Text after equation (10), journal p. 298: if a radix r_j can itself be factored as s_jt_j, replacing it by those two factors never increases the sum of radices and usually decreases it; the equality exception s_j=t_j=2 explains why pairing factors of 2 into radix 4 loses no operations.
Equations (11)–(12), journal p. 298: for equal radix r and N=r^m, m=log_r N and T(r)=rN log_r N.

Equation (13) and the table on journal pp. 298–299: for mixed radices, T/(N log2 N) is a weighted mean of r/log2 r. Among integer radices 2–10, radix 3 is formally best at 1.88, while radices 2 and 4 both give 2.00.

Journal p. 299: radix 3's operation advantage over radix 2 or 4 is only about 6%; radices through 10 cost no more than about 50% over the best listed value, so a highly composite transform length can be chosen within a few percent of a desired large N.
Equations (14)–(19), journal p. 299: for N=2^m, binary digits of j and k define successive arrays A_l in which each stage resolves one two-point sum and exchanges one k digit for one j digit.

Equations (20)–(21), journal p. 300: each radix-2 stage touches only the pair of locations whose indices differ in the active bit. This provides an in-place implementation and exposes stage-level parallelism across all other index bits.
Equation (22), journal p. 300: the final intermediate array contains the desired Fourier sums, but its location index is the bit reversal of the natural output index.

Equations (23)–(25), journal p. 300: the periodic difference equation aX(j+1)+bX(j)+cX(j-1)=F(j) diagonalizes under the Fourier transform, giving A(k)=B(k)/(aW^k+b+cW^(-k)); keeping B and A bit-inverted lets the inverse calculation deliver correctly ordered samples without an isolated bit-reversal pass.

Timing table, journal pp. 300–301: the IBM 7094 program reports 0.02 minutes for 2^11 points, 0.04–0.07 minutes for 2^12, and 0.10–0.13 minutes for 2^13, depending on whether the array is factored across one or three dimensions.
pedagogy: This is a compact primary-source derivation, not a modern tutorial. It moves continuously from the transform definition to a two-factor algebraic decomposition, generalizes the operation count, specializes the indices to binary digits, and closes with one application and one machine-timing table. There are no diagrams, pseudocode listings, named sections, worked exercises, or review questions. The proof style is constructive: substitute mixed-radix indices, identify which terms are independent of the inner summation variable, name the intermediate array, and count every output of each short transform. The radix-2 implementation is expressed entirely in multi-index notation, so contemporary learners benefit from a companion butterfly diagram and a small N=8 trace. The paper assumes comfort with complex Fourier series, roots of unity, nested sums, modular exponents, binary positional notation, logarithms, difference equations, and machine storage/addressing. Its historical wording is pedagogically valuable because it emphasizes constraints still central to FFT design—factorable lengths, arithmetic count, memory reuse, data ordering, and parallelism—without hiding them behind a software-library call.
figures: Recreate equations (3)–(8), journal pp. 297–298, as an r1-by-r2 index grid: map k to (k1,k0), perform r1-point column transforms into A1(j0,k0), then r2-point row transforms into X(j1,j0), with the twiddle factors labeled.
Recreate equations (9)–(13), journal pp. 298–299, as an operation-count comparison: N^2 direct work versus N sum r_i, plus r/log2 r bars for radices 2–10 highlighting 3 at 1.88 and 2/4 at 2.00.
Recreate equations (14)–(19), journal p. 299, as a bit-flow table for N=8: each stage converts one k bit into one j bit in the intermediate-array address.

Recreate equations (20)–(21), journal p. 300, as the canonical radix-2 butterfly: show two locations that differ only in the active bit, their sum/twiddle-weighted difference, and the independent butterflies available in parallel at one stage.
Recreate equation (22), journal p. 300, as an N=8 natural-order/bit-reversed-order mapping table: 000→000, 001→100, 010→010, 011→110, and so on.

Recreate equations (23)–(25), journal p. 300, as a transform-domain solver flow: F(j) → FFT → B(k), divide by aW^k+b+cW^(-k), then a second transform to X(j), annotating how retained bit reversal cancels.
Recreate the journal pp. 300–301 IBM 7094 timing table as a modern log-scale benchmark panel, separating 1D and 3D shapes while retaining the paper's exact point counts and minute values.

gems: Opening paragraph, journal p. 297: the paper does not present fast Fourier computation as appearing from nowhere; it explicitly begins with Yates's factorial-interaction method, Box et al.'s 3^m extension, and Good's sparse-matrix generalization.

Footnote, journal p. 297: the authors thank Richard Garwin for an ‘essential role in communication and encouragement,’ a compact historical reminder that foundational algorithms also depend on people connecting ideas and researchers.

Equations (3)–(8), journal pp. 297–298: the entire speedup first appears from nothing more exotic than writing one index in base (r1,r2), changing summation order, and naming an intermediate array—a strong set piece for showing that an FFT is a factorization, not an approximation.

Text after equation (10), journal p. 298: factors of 2 may be combined in pairs without operation-count loss because 2+2=2×2; this one arithmetic observation motivates radix 4 before any butterfly optimization is discussed.

Radix table, journal p. 299: radix 3 is mathematically best, but only about 6% better than radix 2 or 4. The paper immediately lets architecture—binary addressing and multiplication economy—override a tiny abstract advantage.

Journal p. 299: allowing radices only up to 10 keeps computation within 50% of the formal best and permits a highly composite N within a few percent of almost any desired large length, an early practical argument against fetishizing powers of two.

Equation (20), journal p. 300: the modern butterfly is present without the later standard diagram; the paper describes it operationally as two locations differing in one bit and notes that all other index combinations can execute simultaneously.

Equation (22), journal p. 300: bit reversal is not added as an implementation afterthought—it falls directly out of the order in which output bits replace input bits in the intermediate-array indices.

Equations (23)–(25), journal p. 300: a cyclic three-term difference equation is solved by two Fourier evaluations and pointwise division, and the algorithm's awkward bit-inverted order becomes an optimization because the second transform can undo it.

Timing table, journal pp. 300–301: for 4096 points the 16×16×16 transform took 0.04 minutes while the one-dimensional 4096-point case took 0.07; for 8192 points the listed three-dimensional cases took 0.10–0.12 minutes versus 0.13 for one dimension. The small table makes data layout and dimensional factorization visibly consequential on the IBM 7094.

Footnote, journal p. 300: a multiprocessing circuit by R. E. Miller and S. Winograd used radix 4 as the most practical choice, connecting the algebraic decomposition immediately to parallel hardware design.
